questions: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
Authentication verifies who a user or system is; authorization decides what that identity is allowed to do
Authentication establishes identity (passwords, certificates, tokens); authorization grants or denies access to resources based on that identity's roles and permissions.
An MQ client authenticates with a certificate and is then authorized by authority records to put to ORDERS.IN.
Which component authenticates users to the OpenShift API and web console?
The OpenShift OAuth server, configured with identity providers such as LDAP, OIDC or HTPasswd
The integrated OAuth server issues tokens after authenticating users through configured identity providers.
Corporate users log in to the OpenShift console with Azure AD through an OIDC identity provider.
Cluster login -> OpenShift OAuth. Platform UI login -> Keycloak (16.1.0).
In CP4I 16.1.0, how are enterprise LDAP users enabled to log in to the Platform UI?
By configuring LDAP user federation (or an IdP such as SAML or OIDC) in the Keycloak instance provided by foundational services and assigning CP4I roles to users or groups
By adding users to the MQ authority records
By editing the Platform UI pod
Keycloak federates LDAP or brokers external IdPs. Roles granted there control what users can do in the Platform UI.
The AD group CP4I-Admins maps to the integration administrator role in Keycloak.
Assign roles to groups, not to individual users.
A company wants single sign-on across the CP4I Platform UI using its existing SAML identity provider. Which approach is correct for 16.1.0?
Configure the SAML IdP as an identity provider in Keycloak and map assertions or groups to CP4I roles
Configure SAML in each MQ queue manager
Keycloak brokers SAML or OIDC IdPs, which enables SSO for the Platform UI and the integrated capability UIs that use it.
Okta (SAML) is configured as an IdP in Keycloak, and users get SSO into the Platform UI.
LDAP users can log into the Platform UI but see no instances or actions. What is the MOST likely cause?
Authentication works, but no CP4I roles or permissions are assigned to their users or groups
Login success shows authentication works; empty views indicate missing authorization (role assignments).
Mapping the LDAP group to the integration developer role made the instances visible.
Logs in but sees nothing -> authorization.
Which built-in OpenShift cluster role allows modifying most objects in a namespace but NOT managing roles and role bindings?
edit allows changes to most resources but not RBAC; admin includes managing roles and bindings in the namespace; view is read-only; cluster-admin is full control.
Developers get edit in cp4i-dev; team leads get admin.
Auditors require that developers can view, but not change, production CP4I resources. What should be granted?
The view cluster role through a RoleBinding in the production namespaces
No access, and shared admin credentials

OpenShift ships a built-in 'view' cluster role that grants read-only access to most namespace resources and no access to Secrets. Binding it to the developer group with a RoleBinding in each production namespace gives visibility without the ability to change anything, which satisfies least privilege and auditors.
oc adm policy add-role-to-group view dev-team -n cp4i-prod
A user gets 'Forbidden: User cannot create resource queuemanagers in API group mq.ibm.com in the namespace cp4i-test'. What is needed?
A Role or ClusterRole that permits creating queuemanagers.mq.ibm.com, bound to the user or group in cp4i-test (often the operator provides aggregated roles for edit or admin)
Creating custom resources needs RBAC permissions for that API group and resource. Many operators aggregate permissions into the standard edit and admin roles.
Correct: RBAC for the CR type.
Binding the user to edit in cp4i-test (which aggregates the MQ CR permissions) resolved it.
Forbidden on a CR -> RBAC for that API group and resource.
An organization wants a CI/CD pipeline to deploy CP4I CRs to production while humans have read-only access. Which design is MOST secure?

A dedicated ServiceAccount for the pipeline (for example Argo CD) with a namespace-scoped Role allowing only the CR types and objects it manages, credentials protected and short-lived where possible, with all changes coming from reviewed Git commits and audited
Give the pipeline cluster-admin and a long-lived token
Use a human administrator's personal token in the pipeline
Allow developers to apply changes directly to production
Least-privilege, purpose-specific ServiceAccounts with auditable, reviewed changes give strong control. Personal or over-privileged credentials create risk.
Correct: least-privilege pipeline identity plus GitOps review.
Argo CD's application controller SA has a Role limited to QueueManager, IntegrationRuntime, ConfigMap and Secret in cp4i-prod.
Machine identity + least privilege + reviewed changes.
An identity for processes running in pods to authenticate to the Kubernetes API (and other systems), with permissions granted by RBAC
ServiceAccounts give workloads an identity. Tokens are projected into pods and permissions come from RoleBindings.
The ACE runtime pod uses ServiceAccount ace-runtime with read access to specific Secrets.
A workload does not need to call the Kubernetes API. What is a recommended hardening step?
Set automountServiceAccountToken: false (or use a ServiceAccount with no permissions) so no unnecessary API token is available to the pod
Grant it cluster-admin just in case
Share the default token with other pods

By default Kubernetes mounts a ServiceAccount token into every pod. If the workload never calls the Kubernetes API, that token is only an asset for an attacker who compromises the container. Setting automountServiceAccountToken: false (or using a ServiceAccount with no RoleBindings) removes that path.
Gateway pods that never call the API run without a mounted token.
Reduce attack surface: no token unless needed.
An operator pod logs 'forbidden: cannot list secrets in namespace cp4i-team2' after a team namespace was added for a namespace-scoped install. What is the MOST likely cause?
The operator's OperatorGroup or target namespaces (and therefore its RBAC) do not include cp4i-team2, so it lacks permissions there
OLM grants operator RBAC according to the OperatorGroup's target namespaces. A namespace outside that scope gives the operator no permissions there.
Adding cp4i-team2 to the OperatorGroup target namespaces (or installing the operator there) fixed it.
Operator forbidden errors -> check the OperatorGroup scope.
Are Kubernetes Secrets encrypted by default just because they are Secrets?
No; they are base64-encoded. Encryption at rest requires enabling etcd encryption, and access must be restricted with RBAC
Yes, always with AES-256 by default
Yes, they are hashed and cannot be read
Secrets are stored only in memory
Base64 is encoding, not encryption. OpenShift supports etcd encryption (for example AES-CBC or AES-GCM), and RBAC must restrict who can read Secrets.
Wrong: readable by anyone with access.
The platform team enables etcd encryption and limits get secrets to specific ServiceAccounts.
A bank requires that integration credentials are stored in an enterprise vault, not in Git. Which approach fits best?
Use the External Secrets Operator or a Secrets Store CSI driver to sync or mount secrets from the vault (for example HashiCorp Vault), referencing them from CP4I configurations
Commit Secrets to Git in plain YAML
Vault integrations keep secret values out of Git while still allowing declarative references. Rotation happens centrally.
An ExternalSecret maps vault path kv/cp4i/prod/db to a Kubernetes Secret used by setdbparms.
Never store plaintext secrets in Git.
A database password was rotated in the vault, but the ACE runtime still fails to log in. The Kubernetes Secret shows the new value. What is the likely issue?
The runtime read the credentials at startup; it needs a restart or rollout to pick up the changed configuration
Many runtimes load credentials at startup. After a Secret changes, a restart (or a configuration-triggered rollout) applies it.
The rotation runbook now includes a rolling restart of dependent runtimes after the Secret updates.
Rotation = update the secret + roll the consumers.
Which credential rotation strategy minimizes downtime for integrations that use database credentials?
Dual credentials: create the new credential, update the secret and roll the runtimes so they use it, verify, then revoke the old credential
Revoke the old password first, then update applications
Rotate all credentials on all systems simultaneously without verification
Overlapping validity of old and new credentials allows a rolling switch without failures. Revocation happens after confirming the new credential works.
The database supports two passwords per user during the rotation window.
Rotation without downtime needs an overlap period.
Which cert-manager resource represents a desired certificate that should be issued and renewed automatically?
A Certificate resource describes the desired certificate (DNS names, duration, issuer reference). cert-manager issues it into a Secret and renews it automatically.
Wrong: Issuers sign; they are not the certificate.
Certificate qm1-tls with dnsNames qm1.example.com, issued by ClusterIssuer corp-ca.
Issuer/ClusterIssuer = who signs. Certificate = what to issue.
What is the difference between an Issuer and a ClusterIssuer in cert-manager?
An Issuer can sign certificates only in its own namespace; a ClusterIssuer can be referenced from any namespace

Both are cert-manager signing configurations; they differ only in scope. An Issuer is namespaced and can sign Certificates only in its own namespace. A ClusterIssuer is cluster-scoped and can be referenced from any namespace, which suits a shared enterprise CA used by all CP4I namespaces.
A ClusterIssuer backed by the corporate CA issues certificates for all CP4I namespaces.
Browsers show 'not trusted' warnings when accessing the Platform UI. What is the BEST fix?
Replace the default ingress or route certificate with one issued by a CA trusted by the enterprise (for example a custom certificate for the Platform UI or the ingress wildcard)
Tell users to click through the warning

Browsers trust only certificates that chain to a CA in their trust store. Default self-signed or internal certificates trigger warnings, which train users to click through real attacks. Issue the Platform UI or ingress certificate from a CA the enterprise already trusts (corporate PKI or a public CA).
The Platform UI route uses a certificate from the corporate CA, which is trusted by all managed laptops.
Trust warnings -> issue certificates from trusted CAs.
Clients suddenly fail TLS handshakes with a queue manager, and the error log mentions the certificate has expired. What should have prevented this?
Automated certificate lifecycle management (cert-manager renewal with appropriate renewBefore), plus monitoring and alerting on certificate expiry

Certificates have fixed validity periods. When one expires, TLS handshakes fail and every dependent connection breaks at once. cert-manager can renew certificates automatically (Certificate.spec.renewBefore), and monitoring should alert well before expiry in case renewal fails or certificates are managed elsewhere.
Correct: automated renewal plus expiry alerts.
Certificates renew 30 days before expiry, and alerts fire at 21 days if renewal failed.
Monitor certificate expiry like disk space.
A Certificate resource stays 'Issuing' and is never Ready. The CertificateRequest shows 'issuer not found'. What is the cause?
The Certificate references an Issuer name or kind that does not exist in that namespace (or should reference a ClusterIssuer)
The CA certificate expired 10 years ago
cert-manager cannot sign without the referenced issuer. A namespaced Issuer must exist in the same namespace; otherwise reference a ClusterIssuer with kind: ClusterIssuer.
Changing issuerRef.kind to ClusterIssuer fixed the issuance.
When CP4I instances use certificates from an internal CA, what must be distributed to external clients (MQ apps, Kafka clients, API consumers)?
The CA certificate chain (root and any intermediates) so clients can verify server certificates; for mutual TLS, clients also need their own certificates issued by a CA the server trusts
Clients need the trust chain, never the private key. Mutual TLS adds client certificates trusted by the server.
Correct: trust chain (plus client certificates for mTLS).
Partners receive the corporate root and intermediate certificates to verify the gateway, and their client certificates are signed by the partner CA trusted by DataPower.
Share public certificates freely; protect private keys absolutely.
What does mutual TLS (mTLS) add compared with standard (one-way) TLS?
The client also presents a certificate that the server verifies, so both sides authenticate each other

In standard (one-way) TLS, only the server presents a certificate, so the client verifies the server but the server knows nothing cryptographic about the client. In mutual TLS, the client also presents a certificate that the server validates against trusted CAs. This gives strong, credential-free client authentication, common for B2B and service-to-service traffic.
Partners call the payment API over mTLS; DataPower validates their client certificates.
mTLS = strong client authentication for B2B.
How is a client's TLS certificate mapped to an MQ user identity for authorization?
Using CHLAUTH SSLPEERMAP rules (matching the certificate's distinguished name) to map to an MCAUSER, which is then authorized through authority records
SSLPEERMAP rules map certificate DNs to user IDs, which authority records then authorize. Other certificate-based mapping mechanisms also exist in recent MQ versions.
Correct: SSLPEERMAP to MCAUSER, then authorities.
SET CHLAUTH(APP.SVRCONN) TYPE(SSLPEERMAP) SSLPEER('CN=billing-app') USERSRC(MAP) MCAUSER('billing')
A partner's mTLS calls to the API gateway fail after the partner renewed its client certificate, which is now issued by a new partner CA. What should the gateway team update?
The gateway's TLS server profile validation credentials (trusted CAs for client certificates) to include the partner's new CA
The server must trust the CA that issued client certificates. A new CA requires an update to the trust store.
Wrong: the gateway never holds the partner's private key.
Adding PartnerCA-2025 to the validation credentials restored partner access.
Inbound mTLS trust lives in the server profile's validation credentials.
Which TWO statements about TLS for CP4I traffic are correct? (Select TWO.)
Internal service-to-service traffic should also use TLS where supported (zero trust), not only external traffic
Strong protocol versions (TLS 1.2 or 1.3) and approved cipher suites should be enforced, disabling legacy protocols
TLS is unnecessary inside the cluster because networks are always trusted
SSL 3.0 should be enabled for compatibility
Zero-trust and compliance standards expect encryption in transit everywhere, with modern protocols and ciphers.
Wrong: insider and lateral threats exist.
MQ channels use ANY_TLS13_OR_HIGHER, and Kafka internal listeners use TLS.
A Kafka client fails with 'PKIX path building failed' when connecting to the external Event Streams listener. What is missing?
The client truststore does not contain the CA certificate that signed the Event Streams listener certificate
Java's PKIX error means the server certificate cannot be validated against trusted CAs. Add the cluster CA, downloadable from Event Streams, to the client truststore.
Correct: client truststore missing the CA.
The team downloads the cluster CA from the Event Streams UI and imports it into a PKCS12 truststore.
What is an OAuth 2.0 access token used for?
Presenting to a resource server (API) as proof of authorization granted to a client, often with scopes
Access tokens convey delegated authorization. APIs validate them (introspection or JWT validation) and check scopes.
Wrong: tokens are not password stores.
A mobile app sends 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' with scope accounts:read.
Tokens must travel over TLS. Bearer means whoever has it can use it.
What are the three parts of a JWT (JSON Web Token)?
A JWS-formatted JWT has a base64url-encoded header, claims payload and signature; the signature protects integrity.
The gateway decodes the claims sub, aud and exp after verifying the signature with the IdP's JWKS.
Signed JWTs are readable by anyone; they are not encrypted unless JWE is used.
Which JWT claims should an API gateway validate in addition to the signature?
exp (expiry), iss (issuer), aud (audience), and optionally nbf and scope or roles
None; the signature alone is sufficient
Validating issuer, audience and time-based claims prevents token misuse across APIs or after expiry.
Wrong: a token for another audience could be replayed.
Tokens for the HR API are rejected by the payments API because aud does not match.
Signature + iss + aud + exp = minimum validation.
When should an API gateway use token introspection instead of local JWT validation?
When tokens are opaque (not self-contained) or when near-real-time revocation status must be checked with the authorization server
Always, because JWTs cannot be validated locally
Opaque tokens need introspection. JWTs can be validated locally for performance, but revocation is harder to detect without introspection or short lifetimes.
Correct: opaque tokens or revocation needs.
Wrong: JWTs can be validated locally.
High-risk payment APIs introspect tokens; low-risk catalog APIs validate JWTs locally with 5-minute lifetimes.
JWT local validation = speed. Introspection = freshness.
An API that validates JWTs suddenly rejects all tokens with 'signature invalid', although tokens look correct. The IdP rotated keys this morning. What is the MOST likely cause?
The gateway is using a cached or static public key and does not have the new signing key (kid); configure it to use the IdP's JWKS endpoint, or update the key
After key rotation, validators must obtain the new public key. Using a JWKS URL with kid matching handles rotation automatically.
Switching jwt-validate to a JWKS URL made future rotations seamless.
Key rotation -> JWKS with kid matching.
A company must allow third-party fintechs to access customer account data with customer consent, under open-banking style regulation. Which security architecture is MOST appropriate?

OAuth 2.0 authorization code with PKCE (or FAPI-aligned profiles) with explicit consent capture, mTLS client authentication or private_key_jwt for confidential clients, short-lived access tokens with refresh tokens, fine-grained scopes, and audit of consent and access
Client credentials grant for all fintechs with no user consent
Consent-based delegated access requires user-involved flows, strong client authentication, constrained tokens and auditable consent, as typical of open banking and FAPI profiles.
Correct: consent, strong client authentication, short-lived tokens and scopes.
The bank's API Connect OAuth provider issues accounts:read tokens bound to the fintech's mTLS certificate after the customer consents.
Regulated delegated access -> authorization code + strong client authentication + consent.
How can IBM MQ authenticate application user IDs and passwords against a corporate LDAP directory?
Configure an AUTHINFO object of type IDPWLDAP and set the queue manager's CONNAUTH to use it, then refresh security
CONNAUTH with an IDPWLDAP AUTHINFO object makes MQ validate credentials against LDAP, and can also use LDAP groups for authorization.
MQ validates the billing service account password against AD and authorizes the AD group billing-apps.
MQ connection authentication: IDPWOS (OS) or IDPWLDAP (LDAP).
API Manager login with an LDAP user registry fails for all users after the LDAP team enabled LDAPS only. What should be changed?
Update the API Connect LDAP user registry to use LDAPS (port 636) with a TLS client profile that trusts the LDAP server's CA
When LDAP requires TLS, the registry configuration must use LDAPS and trust the directory's certificate chain.
Correct: LDAPS with a trusted TLS profile.
A TLS client profile with the AD CA is attached to the LDAP registry using port 636.
When a dependency enables TLS, every client must trust its CA.
Why is it better to grant CP4I and OpenShift permissions to LDAP groups rather than to individual users?
Group-based access is easier to manage and audit: joiners and leavers are handled in the directory, and permissions follow group membership

When permissions are granted to directory groups, joiners, movers and leavers are handled in one place, the enterprise directory. Access reviews become group reviews and revocation is immediate. Per-user grants scatter access across many systems and are easily forgotten when people change roles.
Wrong: individual permissions are supported but harder to manage.
Removing a leaver from the cp4i-admins AD group revokes all CP4I admin rights.
LDAP group membership changes are not reflected in OpenShift group-based RBAC. What is required?
Run LDAP group synchronization (oc adm groups sync), for example on a schedule, because OpenShift groups are not automatically live-linked to LDAP groups
OpenShift groups from LDAP are synced on demand or on a schedule, so membership changes need re-sync (or the IdP can supply group claims, depending on configuration).
A CronJob runs groups sync hourly with a whitelist of CP4I-related groups.
LDAP groups in OpenShift need sync.
What is the purpose of an API rate limit in the context of security?
To protect APIs from abuse and overload (for example brute force or denial of service) by limiting how many calls a consumer can make in a period

Rate limits cap how many calls a consumer can make in a time window. Security-wise, they slow brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks, reduce scraping, and blunt application-layer denial of service. They also protect back-end capacity from a single misbehaving client.
A login API allows 5 calls per minute per client to slow credential stuffing.
Rate limiting is a security control as well as a commercial one.
Which control prevents a client from sending unexpected fields or malformed data to a back-end API?
Request validation against the API's schema (for example a validate policy using the OpenAPI definition)
Schema validation at the gateway rejects malformed input early, which reduces injection and parsing risks.
POST /orders bodies that fail the OpenAPI schema receive HTTP 400 from the gateway.
Which TWO measures reduce the risk of sensitive data leaking through API responses and analytics? (Select TWO.)
Redact or remove sensitive fields in API assemblies and analytics logging (for example a redact policy or field-level controls)
Return only the fields consumers need (response shaping and mapping)
Log full request and response bodies for all APIs

Two complementary controls reduce data leakage. Minimization means returning only the fields each consumer needs, for example through response mapping. Redaction means masking or removing sensitive fields where data is still processed or logged, such as in API Connect analytics or activity logs. Logging full payloads does the opposite.
The analytics policy masks card numbers; the response map returns only the last 4 digits.
A browser-based single-page application gets CORS errors calling an API through the gateway, while the same calls from Postman work. What should be configured?
CORS policy on the API (allowed origins, methods, headers) so the gateway answers preflight requests appropriately
Browsers enforce CORS. The API must return the right Access-Control-Allow-* headers for allowed origins. Postman does not enforce CORS.
Enabling CORS for https://app.example.com resolved the browser errors.
Works in Postman but not in the browser -> CORS.

An API exposes customer data. Security review finds that any authenticated user can request any customer's data by changing the ID in the URL. What is this vulnerability, and where should it be fixed?
Broken object-level authorization (BOLA/IDOR); enforce ownership checks in the API implementation (and optionally at the gateway using token claims), not just authentication
BOLA, the top OWASP API risk, needs authorization logic that checks the caller's rights to the specific object, typically in the implementation, informed by token claims.
Wrong: TLS does not fix authorization.
Wrong: slows exploitation but does not fix it.
ACE checks that the token's customer_id claim matches the requested /customers/{id}.
Authentication is not authorization. Check per object.
What does a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy control?
Which pods and namespaces can communicate with selected pods (ingress) and where they can connect (egress), at the network level

A NetworkPolicy selects pods and declares which ingress sources and egress destinations (pods, namespaces, IP blocks and ports) are allowed. The cluster network plugin enforces it; in OpenShift that is OVN-Kubernetes. Without any policy selecting a pod, all traffic to it is allowed.
Only ACE pods may connect to the queue manager's listener port 1414.
No NetworkPolicy = everything allowed by default (unless the platform adds defaults).
A team applies a default-deny ingress NetworkPolicy to the CP4I namespace. Afterwards, Routes stop working. What must be added?
A NetworkPolicy allowing ingress from the OpenShift ingress router (for example namespaces labelled with the ingress policy group) to the exposed pods
Default-deny blocks the router too. Allow traffic from the ingress controller's namespace or policy group.
Correct: allow from the ingress router.
Default deny -> explicitly allow the router, monitoring and the operators' traffic.
After introducing strict NetworkPolicies, CP4I instances stop reconciling and show certificate or connection errors from operators. What was probably blocked?
Traffic between operators (in their namespace) and instance pods, or to required services such as cert-manager webhooks or the API server, which must be explicitly allowed
Operators need network access to instance endpoints for management and health. Webhooks need access as well. Policies must allow these paths.
Correct: operator and webhook paths blocked.
Allowing ingress from the openshift-operators namespace to the instance pods restored reconciliation.
Check documented NetworkPolicy requirements per capability.
Which network segmentation approach BEST supports a zero-trust CP4I design?
Default-deny NetworkPolicies per namespace with explicit allow rules for required flows (router, operators, monitoring, specific client namespaces), plus egress restrictions to approved destinations
A flat network with no policies

Zero trust assumes an attacker may already be inside the network. Default-deny NetworkPolicies, with explicit allow rules only for required flows (router, operators, monitoring, specific clients) and restricted egress, ensure a compromised pod cannot freely reach other workloads or exfiltrate data.
Correct: default deny + explicit allows + egress control.
Only the payments namespace may reach the payments queue manager; egress is restricted to the partner CIDRs.
Zero trust = deny by default, allow by need.
Which OpenShift feature restricts which external destinations pods in a namespace can reach?

Egress controls restrict where pods can connect outbound. In OpenShift with OVN-Kubernetes, an EgressFirewall allows or denies traffic to CIDR ranges or DNS names per namespace, and egress NetworkPolicy rules add pod-level control. This is a key defence against data exfiltration.
cp4i-prod may only reach the partner API IP range and the corporate database subnet.
What do Security Context Constraints (SCCs) control in OpenShift?
What security-related settings pods may use, for example running as root, privilege escalation, host access, capabilities and SELinux context
SCCs define allowed pod security attributes. CP4I is designed to run under restricted SCCs (restricted-v2 on current OpenShift).
CP4I pods run as non-root with random UIDs under restricted-v2.
Never grant anyuid or privileged without strong justification.
A custom ACE image fails to start under the restricted-v2 SCC because it expects to run as root and write to /opt owned by root. What is the right fix?
Rebuild the image to run as a non-root, arbitrary UID with group-writable directories (GID 0 permissions), following OpenShift image guidelines
Run the pod on a control plane node
OpenShift assigns random UIDs that belong to group 0. Images should set group permissions accordingly rather than require root.
Correct: fix the image for arbitrary UIDs.
chgrp -R 0 /home/aceuser && chmod -R g=u /home/aceuser in the Dockerfile.
Fix the image, not the SCC.
Which TWO practices strengthen container runtime security for CP4I workloads? (Select TWO.)
Run containers as non-root with dropped Linux capabilities and no privilege escalation
Use read-only root file systems where supported, writing only to explicit volumes
Mount the host's Docker socket into pods
Run all pods with the privileged SCC

Container hardening limits what an attacker can do after compromising a process. Running as non-root, dropping Linux capabilities, disabling privilege escalation and using a read-only root file system remove common escalation paths. Mounting host sockets or using privileged SCCs gives node-level control.
A security baseline requires allowPrivilegeEscalation: false and drop: ALL for custom images.
Least privilege inside the container too.
Why should container images be scanned for vulnerabilities?
To detect known CVEs in operating system packages and libraries before and after deployment, so risky images can be fixed or blocked
Scanning identifies known vulnerabilities. Continuous scanning catches newly disclosed CVEs in running images.
Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security flags a critical CVE in a custom ACE image's base layer.
Scan at build, at admission and continuously.
Which approach BEST prevents deployment of images with critical vulnerabilities into production namespaces?
Enforce admission policies (for example with Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security) that block images exceeding a severity threshold or lacking a signature, with exceptions governed
Admission-time enforcement makes policy non-optional, and an exception process handles necessary deviations.
ACS blocks deployment of images with fixable critical CVEs in cp4i-prod.
A scanner reports a critical CVE in an IBM CP4I product image currently in production. What is the MOST appropriate response?

Check IBM security bulletins for the CVE's applicability and fix availability, apply the recommended fix pack or operand version (or mitigation) through the normal upgrade path, and track the exception until resolved
Modify the IBM image yourself to remove the package
Vendor images are patched through vendor fix packs. Modifying product images is unsupported. Bulletins clarify whether the CVE is exploitable in context.
Correct: vendor bulletins plus supported upgrade.
The bulletin lists an MQ fix level; the team updates spec.version after testing.
Vendor CVE -> bulletin -> supported fix -> track.
How can an organization verify that the CP4I images running in its cluster are authentic and unmodified?
Pull images by digest from trusted registries and verify image signatures (IBM signs CP4I images) using a signature verification policy
Digests are immutable content identifiers; signatures prove origin. Together they protect the supply chain.
Correct: digest pinning plus signature verification.
A cluster image policy verifies IBM signatures for cp.icr.io/cp/* images.
Tag = label. Digest = content. Signature = origin.
What do OpenShift API server audit logs record?
Requests made to the Kubernetes and OpenShift API (who did what, when, to which resource), according to the audit policy profile
Audit logs provide accountability for cluster changes. The policy profile controls detail, for example whether request bodies are logged.
Investigators trace who deleted a QueueManager CR using the audit log.
Forward audit logs to a SIEM; they rotate on nodes.
How can MQ administrators audit configuration changes and authorization failures?
Enable MQ event messages (for example configuration, command and authority events) and collect them for monitoring and SIEM
MQ emits event messages to system event queues for configuration changes, commands and authorization failures. These can be forwarded to monitoring or SIEM tools.
Authority events reveal repeated 2035 failures from an unknown application ID.
Enable AUTHOREV, CONFIGEV and CMDEV for auditing.
A security team requires a centralized audit trail across CP4I. Which TWO sources should be collected? (Select TWO.)
OpenShift API audit logs (changes to CRs, Secrets and RBAC)
Product-level audit and security events (for example API Connect management audit logs, MQ authority and command events, identity provider login events)

A complete audit trail needs platform events (OpenShift API audit logs showing changes to CRs, Secrets and RBAC) and product events (API Connect management audit, MQ command and authority events, identity provider logins). Centralizing them in a SIEM allows correlation and tamper-resistant retention.
Correct: product and identity audit events.
The SIEM correlates a Keycloak login, an OpenShift CR change and an MQ command event for one change.
Audit at every layer, then centralize.
Auditors ask who changed a Secret's value last week, but the audit records show only metadata, not request bodies. Why?
The audit policy profile (for example Default) does not record request bodies; profiles such as WriteRequestBodies record write payloads, at the cost of sensitivity and volume
OpenShift audit profiles control the detail level. Logging bodies increases data sensitivity and size, so it is a trade-off.
Wrong: metadata exists, so logging is on.
The team retains metadata-level audits centrally and relies on vault audit logs for secret value changes.
Choose the audit profile deliberately; payloads can contain secrets.
Which combination protects sensitive integration data in transit, at rest and in logs?
TLS on all connections, storage encryption with key management, and masking or redaction of sensitive fields in logs and analytics

Sensitive integration data exists in three states. In transit it needs TLS. At rest it needs storage encryption with managed keys. In observability pipelines (logs, traces, analytics) it needs masking or redaction. TLS alone leaves data exposed on disk and in logs; base64 is only an encoding.
Card data travels over mTLS, is encrypted on disk by ODF with KMS, and is redacted in API analytics.
Regulations require that MQ administrators must not be able to read payment payloads on queues, even with full MQ admin rights. Which solution meets this?
MQ Advanced Message Security (AMS) with privacy (encryption) policies, so only authorized applications holding the keys can decrypt payloads
Restricting browse access through authority records only
TLS protects the network hop; disk encryption protects media; authority records can be changed by admins. AMS encrypts the message payload end to end, so administrators cannot read it.
Wrong: data is decrypted at the queue manager.
Wrong: the OS or admin sees plaintext.
The payments queue uses an AMS privacy policy listing only the payments app's certificate as a recipient.
Which approach allows sharing a Kafka topic containing PII with an analytics partner while complying with data minimization rules?
Expose the topic through EEM with a redaction control that removes PII fields for that partner's option, plus approval and auditing of the subscription
Copy the topic and remove fields manually each night
Gateway-enforced redaction per subscription option supports data minimization without separate pipelines.
The 'analytics-partner' option removes name, email and phone fields from order events.
Redact at the access point per consumer.
Where should edge security functions (WAF, DDoS protection, API threat protection) sit in a CP4I internet-facing architecture?
In front of or at the gateway layer (CDN/WAF, then the DataPower API gateway in a DMZ), so attacks are filtered before reaching internal integration runtimes
Nowhere; Kubernetes is secure by default

Edge controls such as a CDN or WAF (DDoS protection, OWASP rules) followed by a hardened API gateway (authentication, schema validation, threat protection, rate limits) stop malicious traffic before it reaches integration runtimes and back ends. Defence in depth means each layer catches what earlier layers miss.
Internet -> cloud WAF -> DataPower in DMZ cluster -> ACE in internal cluster.
Defend in layers from the edge inward.
A bank wants to place internet-facing CP4I components separately from internal ones. Which architecture BEST supports this?

A separate DMZ cluster (or dedicated nodes with a separate ingress shard and network zone) hosting gateways (DataPower API Gateway, EEM Event Gateway), with only required, firewalled, mTLS-protected connections into the internal cluster where ACE, MQ and Event Streams run
All components in one namespace exposed through one route
Expose MQ and Kafka brokers directly to the internet
Put the management UIs on the public internet for convenience
Network zoning minimizes exposure: only gateways face the internet, and internal components are reachable only through controlled paths.
The DMZ cluster has two ingress paths (public, partner) and one allowed egress to the internal gateway services.
Only gateways at the edge; everything else stays internal.
A penetration test finds that the ACE administration REST API and the MQ web console are reachable from the corporate network by anyone. What should be done?
Restrict administrative endpoints: require authentication with role-based access, limit network exposure (no public routes, NetworkPolicies and ingress restrictions), and enforce TLS
Administrative interfaces are high-value targets. Combine strong authentication, authorization and network restriction.
Admin routes are removed; administrators reach consoles only through the Platform UI with SSO, from an admin network.
Admin planes should never be broadly exposed.
Which TWO principles should guide a CP4I security architecture? (Select TWO.)
Least privilege for users, workloads and network paths
Defence in depth across edge, platform, product and data layers
Least privilege and defence in depth are foundational. Shared accounts and late reviews undermine security.
Threat modelling during design identified the need for AMS on payment queues.
Security by design, not by retrofit.

A client connecting to Event Streams receives 'SaslAuthenticationException: Authentication failed during authentication due to invalid credentials with SASL mechanism SCRAM-SHA-512'. What should be checked?
That the username and password come from the correct KafkaUser Secret, the KafkaUser exists and is Ready, and the listener is configured for SCRAM

SCRAM-SHA-512 authentication fails when the username or password does not match a KafkaUser's credentials. Common causes are using an old Secret after the user was recreated or the password rotated, a KafkaUser that is not Ready, or connecting to a listener configured for a different mechanism such as mTLS.
The client was using the password of an old KafkaUser that had been recreated with a new Secret.
Authentication errors -> credentials or mechanism. Authorization errors -> ACLs.
What does the default MQ CHLAUTH rule that blocks '*MQADMIN' on client channels achieve?
It prevents remote clients from connecting with privileged administrative user IDs unless explicitly allowed
MQ blocks privileged users over client channels by default, which reduces the risk of remote administrative misuse.
Correct: blocks privileged remote access by default.
A developer connecting as 'mqm' over a client channel is rejected with 2035.
Do not remove the default protections; map to non-privileged users instead.
How can API Connect restrict an API operation to callers whose OAuth token contains a specific scope?
Define the scope in the OAuth security definition and require it on the operation, so the gateway checks the token's scopes
Scopes link tokens to permitted operations. The gateway enforces required scopes before invoking the back end.
Scopes are coarse-grained authorization at the gateway.
Which design gives consistent identity across the OpenShift console, the CP4I Platform UI and product UIs?
Use the same enterprise IdP (for example OIDC or SAML through Keycloak for CP4I and OIDC for OpenShift OAuth), with group-based role mappings maintained in the enterprise directory
Separate local user databases in every component
Federating all components to the enterprise IdP gives SSO, central lifecycle management and consistent group-based authorization.
Azure AD backs both OpenShift OAuth and Keycloak; AD groups drive roles everywhere.
Card numbers were found in API Connect analytics records. What should be done?

Configure analytics data redaction or removal for sensitive fields (and adjust the API's logging and activity-log settings to avoid capturing payloads), then purge or retain existing data according to policy
API activity logging can capture payloads. Configure redaction and logging levels, and handle the existing data per compliance policy.
Correct: redact, reduce logging and remediate data.
Activity logging is set to header-only for card APIs, with a redact rule for $.card.number.
Observability pipelines need data protection controls.
Which OpenShift operator helps assess cluster configuration against security benchmarks such as CIS?
The Compliance Operator scans nodes and the platform against profiles (for example CIS or NIST) and can remediate.
Monthly CIS scans report the cluster's compliance posture to auditors.
Which Event Streams listener authentication options are typically available for external clients?
SCRAM-SHA-512 (username and password over TLS), mutual TLS certificates, or OAuth (depending on configuration)
Event Streams listeners can be configured for SCRAM, mTLS or OAuth authentication, all over TLS for external access.
Wrong: insecure and unsuitable for external access.
Wrong: not a Kafka protocol mechanism.
Internal apps use mTLS; partner apps use SCRAM through EEM credentials.
Pick an authentication mechanism per listener and audience.
Why might an architect configure CP4I to use certificates from a corporate CA (ClusterIssuer) instead of default self-signed CAs?
So clients across the enterprise trust CP4I endpoints with existing trust stores, to satisfy security policy, and to centralize certificate governance and revocation
Self-signed certificates encrypt but require distributing custom trust. A corporate CA integrates with existing trust and governance.
Wrong: CP4I uses them by default.
The ClusterIssuer is backed by the enterprise PKI through an ACME or Vault issuer.
An integration platform must support both human SSO for administrators and machine-to-machine access for 300 applications across MQ, Kafka and APIs. Which identity strategy is MOST appropriate?

Humans through the enterprise IdP with MFA and group-based roles; applications through dedicated, least-privilege machine identities per capability (MQ certificates mapped through CHLAUTH, KafkaUsers or EEM subscriptions, OAuth client credentials or mTLS for APIs), with automated provisioning, rotation and ownership metadata
One shared service account for all applications
Separate human and machine identity models, each least-privilege, automated and owned, scale securely.
Correct: separate, least-privilege, automated identity models.
A self-service portal provisions per-app MQ certificates and KafkaUsers with 90-day rotation.
Humans: SSO + MFA. Machines: per-app credentials + rotation.
After applying an egress default-deny policy, ACE flows fail to resolve hostnames. What must be allowed?
Egress to the cluster DNS service (for example openshift-dns on port 53/5353) in addition to the required destinations
Access to the image registry only

A default-deny egress policy blocks all outbound traffic, including DNS lookups to the cluster DNS service. Pods then fail to resolve any hostname, even ones they are allowed to reach. Add an explicit egress rule to the openshift-dns pods (port 5353 TCP/UDP, or 53 depending on configuration) alongside the required destinations.
Adding an allow rule to the openshift-dns namespace on UDP and TCP 5353 fixed name resolution.
Why should API keys (client IDs and secrets) never be embedded in public mobile or browser application code as the only security control?
They can be extracted easily; public clients need user-based OAuth flows (authorization code + PKCE) and the client ID only identifies the app, not a trusted secret

Mobile and browser applications are public clients: anyone can unpack or inspect them and extract embedded strings. A client secret shipped in such code is not confidential. The client ID only identifies the app. User-level security must come from OAuth flows such as authorization code with PKCE.
Correct: secrets in public clients are not secret.
The mobile app uses PKCE; the client ID only identifies the app.
A security review shows every application uses the same KafkaUser with access to all topics. What is the risk and the remediation?

No least privilege or accountability: a compromise exposes all topics and actions cannot be attributed; create per-application KafkaUsers (or EEM subscriptions) with topic- and group-scoped ACLs, and rotate the shared credential
There is no risk because Kafka is internal
Shared credentials violate least privilege and auditability. Per-application identities with scoped ACLs fix both.
Correct: per-app identities with scoped ACLs.
Forty KafkaUsers replace the shared one; ACLs restrict each to its topics and groups.
A vendor asks for its integration sidecar to run privileged in CP4I namespaces. What should the architect do?

Challenge and assess the requirement: seek a non-privileged alternative; if unavoidable, isolate it (dedicated namespace or nodes, a custom SCC with the minimum capabilities, monitoring) with a documented risk acceptance
Grant privileged across all CP4I namespaces
Run it as root on control plane nodes
Privileged containers can compromise nodes. Least privilege, isolation and formal risk acceptance are required if it cannot be avoided.
The vendor delivered a version that needs only NET_BIND_SERVICE, granted through a custom SCC.
Privileged = node-level risk. Avoid it or isolate it.
